newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslems agree to leave disputed frontline village.
newsitem.headline: Moslems agree to leave disputed frontline village.

text.p: International mediators on Thursday persuaded Moslem refugees who resettled a disputed village on Serb territory two weeks ago to withdraw and return with proper paperwork in three days time.

"The villagers have agreed to leave Jusici and will be accommodated in a tented compound erected by the UNHCR on the (Moslem-Croat) federation side of the line," a NATO spokesman in Sarajevo, Major Simon Haselock, told Reuters.
More than 100 Moslem men, claiming to be former residents of Jusici, crossed former frontlines 13 days ago to reclaim homes in the village.
Some of them carried weapons, in clear violation of the Dayton accord banning arms inside the so-called "zone-of- separation," a belt of demilitarised land dividin the former warring factions.

NATO-led peacekeeping troops confiscated the weapons and sealed off the village to prevent conflicts with Serbs. NATO, the UNHCR and international police then held extensive negotiations to persuade the Moslems to leave.
"We are very pleased to be able to resolve this peacefully," U.S. General George Casey, who took part in the talks, told Reuters.

Under the agreement, three people would stay in the village to watch over the houses until Sunday when all villagers would be allowed to go back with authorised paperwork. Casey said 101 people had so far applied to settle in the village.
A Reuters reporter who visited Jusici said people started leaving in the afternoon, carrying bundles of belongings down a muddy track on a steep hill in driving rain.
"I am filled with pain and sorrow. I've been here for 12 days and now they are driving us out again," said Fatija Ibrahimovic, 51, sobbing and wiping her eyes.
"We agreed to this under international pressure, but only for the sake of Bosnia and all the refugees," said Nekir Islamovic, 31, the village head. "But we shall return here by any means available."
Not all the villagers were convinced that everyone who signed the formal agreement would honour it.

"I am afraid we might get fooled again. The Serbs tricked us once in 1992 and killed 50 of our people," said Rifat Hasanovic, referring to the Serb militia's capture of Jusici at the outset of the Bosnian war.

The Dayton peace accords, which halted the war in December, guaranteed freedom of movement and the right to return to all refugees. But only a few hundred people, most of them Moslems, have ventured across former frontlines to their pre-war homes
